articles.title: SQLite or PostgreSQL: one codebase, two engines, one env var
articles.excerpt: Most boilerplates pick one database and bake it in. GoVueKit supports both, DB_DRIVER, and the same SQL runs on either. This post explains Development. SQLite means make dev works on a fresh laptop wi…
articles.body: Most boilerplates pick one database and bake it in. GoVueKit supports both, selected by DB_DRIVER , and the same SQL runs on either. This post explains how that is done, what it costs, and — the part that actually matters — when SQLite is a legitimate production choice rather than a toy. Why bother supporting both Development. SQLite means make dev works on a fresh laptop with no service to install, no container to start, no credentials to invent. The file is created and migrated on first run. Small production. A single-server product with a few thousand users and read-heavy traffic runs perfectly on SQLite, with backups that are a file copy. Tests that mean something. CI runs the entire Go suite twice, once per engine.

articles.title: What a Licence Under an Image Format Costs You
articles.excerpt: Somebody puts a licence under an image format every few years, and everybody else starts converting. Convertio runs its heic to jpg conversion entirely on its own servers, taking a file of up to 1 GB…
articles.body: Somebody puts a licence under an image format every few years, and everybody else starts converting. Convertio runs its heic to jpg conversion entirely on its own servers, taking a file of up to 1 GB and handing back a JPEG that opens on any device with nothing installed locally. The League for Programming Freedom called for Burn All GIFs Day on 5 November 1999, at the Unisys headquarters, where GIF users would gather and burn their files. Unisys had a patent lawyer named Mark Starr, and The Industry Standard quoted him on 25 April 2000. "They want everything to be free and let's all be friends," he said. "But fortunately, this is not the American way." The patent expired in the United States on 20 June 2003. Canada followed on 7 July 2004.

articles.title: How We Designed an Incident Agent
articles.excerpt: How We Built an Incident Response Agent That Stops Repeating the Same Mistakes Using Hindsight We built OpsMind to kill that cycle. What the System Does The full flow looks like this: An incident is i…
articles.body: How We Built an Incident Response Agent That Stops Repeating the Same Mistakes Using Hindsight There's a bug that lives in almost every ops team I've worked with. Not in the codebase — in the process. An engineer gets paged at 2am. The database is melting. They fix it — increase the connection pool from 20 to 50, write a postmortem, close the ticket. Two months later, a different engineer gets the same page. Different shift. Different memory. Same fix. Same 45 minutes wasted. We built OpsMind to kill that cycle. What the System Does OpsMind is an incident response agent backed by Hindsight — a biomimetic memory layer for AI agents. When a production incident arrives, OpsMind doesn't just suggest generic fixes.

articles.title: Why a shopping cart can't price a hotel stay
articles.excerpt: If you have ever tried to sell hotel stays through a regular e-commerce stack, you hit the wall fast. A product has a price. A hotel night does not: it has a contract. While building FullTravel, a Saa…
articles.body: If you have ever tried to sell hotel stays through a regular e-commerce stack, you hit the wall fast. A product has a price. A hotel night does not: it has a contract. While building FullTravel , a SaaS for independent inbound agencies and tour operators, I had to model what hotels actually send. Here is the list of concepts a pricing engine has to understand before it can quote a single stay correctly: Board basis : room only, bed and breakfast, half board, full board. The same room has a different net rate for each. Seasons and periods : rates change by date range, and a stay that crosses two periods has to be priced night by night, not with one rate. Occupancy : the rate for a room depends on how many adults are in it.

articles.body: At WWDC this year, in the keynote, Apple confirmed something I had been holding as a logical intuition more than as an open question: when the assistant that lives in your phone wants to do something for you, it goes into the apps installed on that phone. An app declares the actions it can perform, and that is what Siri calls. On Android, Google is building the same door under the name AppFunctions, and describes it in its own documentation as the on-device equivalent of the tools an agent calls over MCP. Two operating systems, the same year, the same decision. Meanwhile what you keep reading in 2026 is that apps are on their way out.

articles.title: NASA Armstrong Celebrates 80 Years of Flight Innovation
articles.excerpt: On Sept. 30, 1946, five National Advisory Committee of Aeronautics (NACA) engineers arrived at Muroc Army Airfield in California’s high desert to achieve supersonic flight for the first time. In less…
articles.body: On Sept. 30, 1946, five National Advisory Committee of Aeronautics (NACA) engineers arrived at Muroc Army Airfield in California’s high desert to achieve supersonic flight for the first time. In less than two years, NACA flew the X-1 aircraft faster than the speed of sound, marking an important milestone in aviation history. Fast forward 80 years, and that former NACA outpost is now NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California, flying the X-59 supersonic X-plane in the same skies to demonstrate that supersonic flight doesn’t have to come with a boom. Over Armstrong’s 80-year history, the center has supported milestone missions ranging from space shuttle landings to SR-71 flights, shaping the evolution of science, aeronautics, and space research.
